power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("P<0.05", "P < 0.05", "P<0.05"), 
    Text = c("Of these, 1,494 were associated with the PGS after Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the 2,328 outcomes (q<0.05), including 423 with nominally significant and directionally similar within-family associations (P<0.05, Figure 2A).", 
    "Rumors damaging social reputation Friends who are athletes Overwhelming emotions Sudden mood changes Sad or depressed most of the day Able to concentrate Daytime sleepiness Days with ≥60 min of physical activity Can find a way to feel better when upset A Parent Youth Teacher P < 0.05 within-family Otherwise -0.1 -0.1 0 0 0.1 0.1 0.2 0.2 B Equal effects Fitted profile Slope 1.01 95% CI 0.66-1.35 6.7% 23.3% 0 15 30 Suicidal thoughts 3.5x 1 2 4 10 13 16 6.9% 20.5% 0 15 30 Nonsuicidal self-injury 3.0x 1 2 4 10 13 16 2.4% 7.3% 0 7.5 15 Current social anxiety 3.0x 1 8 64 10 13 16 1.0% 5.0% 0 5 10 Current major depression 5.1x 1 8 64 10 13 16 25.1% 46.9% 0 30 60 Nicotine or cannabis use 1.9x 1 4 16 10 13 16 0.8% 3.8% 0 5 10 Psychiatric inpatient treatment 4.8x 1 8 64 10 13 16 C Bottom PGS decile Top PGS decile Probability (%) RR Probability (%) RR Age (years) Sibling population coefficient Within-family coefficient", 
    "More opaque points have samedirection nominally significant within-family associations (P<0.05)."
    )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "P = 0.08", Sentence = "For the symptom profile, point estimates suggested somewhat stronger associations under disadvantage, but none remained significant after Holm correction (Holm, 1979) across the three exposures (smallest adjusted P = 0.08)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::
